accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are correctly scoped: flat keys/metadata, separate database publication, atomic replacement versus retention, provider consistency boundaries, uncertain uploads, durability versus availability, application authorization and workload roles. Critical claims checked against live AWS/GCS documentation.

evidence.quote: Complete old or new bytes is one guarantee; retaining both is another.

mechanisms.reason: Cards 1-2 explain key prefixes and upload/reference actors; cards 3-5 trace replacement, paginated observations and timeout/retry races; cards 6-7 connect replication and credential scope to concrete failures; card 8 connects interface operations to use cases.

evidence.quote: Verify the intended object, not just the existence of its key.

coherence.reason: The prerequisites are supplied in order across all eight cards, with later uncertainty and retention explanations building on earlier write boundaries. Inspected diagram source: the separate object/reference writes and unresolved conditional response diagrams agree with text. Shared renderer/CSS inspected only, not executed.

evidence.quote: Publishing a reference is a separate decision from storing the bytes.

decisions.reason: Provides actionable publication verification, conditional-write protection, retention/placement checks and scoped authorization, then selects object/database/block/file/CDN roles with whole-object mutation costs.

evidence.quote: Choose the interface for the operations you need, then verify its guarantees.

clarity.reason: Storage terms and comparisons are taught directly. Cards 4-6 carry many important caveats and are fairly dense, but remain understandable with the stated HTTP/database prerequisites.

evidence.quote: The bucket and key locate an object; the application gives its bytes meaning.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria satisfied: learner defines bucket/key/metadata and flat prefixes, traces object/database/reference retrieval, keeps commits separate, permits safe pending records, and explains orphan/missing-byte failures plus application recovery.
All three criteria satisfied: complete replacement, old-or-new single-object reads/current replacement and separate configured retention are explained with provider scope.

All four criteria satisfied: exact-key/prefix versus field-query access and cost, scoped strong reads/listing despite errors/caches, pagination/multi-key transaction limits and overlapping response-order ambiguity.

All three criteria satisfied: timeout uncertainty, unwanted retry overwrite, intended identity/content verification rather than existence, later-read limits, conditional protections and remaining uncertainty/provider differences.
All three criteria satisfied: durability/availability/acknowledgment separation, storage class/zone failure scope, and enabled/effective/retained recovery protections distinct from redundancy.

All seven criteria satisfied: presented storage credential versus user ownership, obscure-key and credential-scope limits, revocation propagation, object whole-write tradeoff/small-object support, database/block/file roles, and CDN copies versus durable origin.

sourceChecks.claim: Live S3 key documentation establishes flat bucket/key names, prefix/delimiter console folders and metadata. Live GCS objects explicitly describes copying/deleting each flat-prefix object as non-atomic and scopes hierarchical namespaces separately.

Live S3 Welcome describes objects/metadata and key-based single-object operations without atomic cross-key updates; separate external database commits therefore require application coordination. Diagram and text correctly keep pending references distinct from ready publication.

Live GCS Objects immutability section explicitly requires replacement and serves old bytes until atomic replacement completes; live S3 Welcome confirms old-or-new reads. Configured versioning/retention is separate, as supported by S3 data protection.

Live GCS consistency and S3 Welcome confirm strong reads/listing, possible request errors, caches and no multi-key transaction. S3 concurrent examples reject acknowledgment arrival as final-value order. GCS list pageToken caveats support non-frozen pagination.

Live GCS preconditions explains generation match, zero matching no live version, 412 rejection and retry races. Live S3 conditional-writes documents If-None-Match/If-Match and their differing conditions. Presence/rejection cannot identify the intended earlier write.

Live GCS availability/durability distinguishes availability from intact data, redundant writes before confirmation and zonal-loss risk; S3 protection/Welcome support redundancy and separate versioning. GCS consistency documents delayed configuration effectiveness. Lost response remains a client knowledge boundary.

Live GCS IAM describes principal roles, resources and permissions; consistency documents eventual grant/revoke propagation. These support checking service credentials separately from application ownership and limiting broad credential exposure.

Live AWS comparison supports object/block/shared-file interfaces; PostgreSQL transaction documentation supports database responsibilities. CloudFront Introduction confirms edge caches and S3 origin retrieval. GCS objects supports arbitrary sizes and whole replacement.
